props.title: Operation Petticoat

sections.content: Operation Petticoat stands as a masterclass in combining wartime comedy with romantic farce, starring Cary Grant and Tony Curtis at their charismatic peaks. The film cleverly subverts WWII submarine movie tropes established by serious works like Run Silent, Run Deep (1958) and The Enemy Below (1957). Director Blake Edwards brings his signature light touch, perfecting the balance of military procedure with screwball situations years before he'd hit even bigger with The Pink Panther (1963). The pink submarine itself becomes an inspired visual gag that keeps giving.

sections.content: The film established a template for military comedy that influenced decades of productions. **M*A*S*H** (1970) would later perfect the mix of service humor and anti-war sentiment, while Down Periscope (1996) directly borrowed Operation Petticoat's submarine-comedy framework. The film particularly shines in its treatment of its female characters, who prove more capable than their male counterparts - progressive for 1959.

Cary Grant's performance as Lieutenant Commander Sherman marks one of his last great comedy roles before transitioning to more dramatic parts. His trademark timing and exasperated reactions ground the increasingly absurd situations, much as he did in Arsenic and Old Lace (1944). Tony Curtis, who had actually served on a submarine during WWII, brings authentic detail to his charming con-man role. SUBHEAD: Impact on Military Comedy Genre

sections.content: The film's influence rippled through Hollywood's treatment of military comedy. Its success helped pave the way for shows like McHale's Navy (1962-1966) and films like Stripes (1981). The formula of mixing service protocol with romantic complications and screwball elements became a reliable template. Even modern entries like Down Periscope (1996) and Renaissance Man (1994) owe a debt to Operation Petticoat's perfect balance of respect for service while mining military life for laughs.
